title: Notes of Ministry - 33 - August 1975

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 33 - August 197 (2412)/Notes of Ministry - 33 - August - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: These scriptures speak about two debtors and two malefactors. Luke is a most encouraging gospel to say a word from because of the rich way in which it deals with the compassions of God in the gospel. All through this gospel we have remarkable references to God’s saving grace, and the wonderful way in which God looks upon the needs of humanity. In the Person of Jesus He identifies Himself with the needs of humanity in a compassion that greatly affects you as you go through the gospel. Whether there are persons deeply sunk in sin, whether they are guilty of crime, whether they have denied God His rights, all through this gospel we get the great thought of the world standing in reconciliation, as contemplating the death of Christ, and man standing provisionally in God’s favour. The Lord Jesus comes into this world, according to this gospel, and takes His place on the side of humanity.

So the title of the Lord in this gospel is Son of man. It is not Son of God, although this is referred to more than once, but it involves as Son of man what the Lord is as coming in on the side of men to take up the matters that involve men and involve humanity, in regard not only to sins, but also death, disease, and demon. We find how the Lord in the service of the glad tidings, as setting it on, identifies Himself with every need common to humanity. Luke speaks so attractively of the Lord coming into the world, coming in in a way that tends to attract souls to Him. Yet, too, He comes in in a way that awakens man’s hatred of God. In one part, early in this gospel, after He had spoken so attractively of being anointed to preach glad tidings to the different categories of weakness that mark humanity, they led Him to the brow of the hill and were going to cast Him down.

Each of these two sections deals with two persons—one is attracted to Jesus and to God as known in Jesus, and the other does not seem to have any proper affinity of feeling in connection with God and His actions in Jesus. This seventh chapter of Luke deals with the woman who was a sinner of the city, in Simon the Pharisee’s house. You never can trust the Simons—religious people are the most difficult to deal with, as this chapter shows. What a difficult man Simon was! And yet I suppose he thought he was doing the best he could to entertain the Lord. But, over against Simon, there was this woman of the city. She is one of the most attractive personalities in this gospel. It is remarkable as you read through Luke’s gospel how he speaks of widows and of how he speaks of young persons. He speaks of a girl, a maiden. He speaks of a boy whom death had claimed. Luke is most attractive in the way he draws our attention to God in Jesus dealing with these conditions in this scene where so much exists that is opposed to God in His operations in grace.

So this matter of the two debtors comes up. Debt is quite a thing in the world today. There have been more bankruptcies this year than there have been for quite a few years. I was noticing the statistics the other day concerning bankruptcies in Michigan. People have got into debt in such a way that they cannot liquidate themselves; they cannot clear themselves. It is bad enough in business when that happens, but what the Lord is really at here is persons who are sinners. The two debtors refer to this. I wonder how much we have felt being in debt in regard to sin. It is a great matter that we should get fully clear in regard to indebtedness to sin. The epistle to the Romans brings up the matter of sin and sins and tells us that “All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God”, Romans 3: 23. It is a great thing that we should not be light in regard to our sins and getting cleared from them. It is a great thing that there should be with us a full experience of having had to do with God about our sins, like this woman who had to do with the Lord about her sins in Simon the Pharisee’s house.

The Lord says to Simon, “I have somewhat to say to thee”. Think of the Lord saying that to some of us. Think of Him saying to you or to me, ‘I have somewhat to say to thee’. I am sure none of us here would say, ‘Well, I do not care to listen’. Simon listened. The Lord says, “There were two debtors of a certain creditor—one owed five hundred denarii and the other fifty; but as they had nothing to pay, he forgave both of them their debt”. This is the wonder of the gospel. When it comes to bankruptcy it is a question of whether you can pay fifty per cent, or forty per cent, or maybe just ten per cent. But when you come to the gospel you have to do with a forgiving God who is ready to forgive us when we do not have anything to pay.

It is a wonderful thing to have a sense of how God has taken us up, and how God has forgiven us all our sins. The Lord said to Simon, “Which of them therefore will love him most?”. It is remarkable how the Lord brings in the matter of love in regard to this thought of forgiveness. Perhaps we have not thought too much about love entering into the matter of forgiveness, but it is a great thing to be affected by what God has done in Christ in this matter of forgiving us our debt. We think of what it cost God, the clearing of the way for redemption, the forsaking of Christ on the cross, the shedding of His blood on the cross.

Think of all that enters into the greatness of the operations that were involved in our being cleared of all the debt that our sins incurred. All the liabilities were taken upon Jesus, and He bore them on the cross.

Simon answered, “I suppose he to whom he forgave the most”. I wonder who amongst us here would come in under the heading of “the most”. I wonder what we feel about the sins we have been forgiven. It humbles us to think of our history and the ways of God, and the matter of the sins that have attached to our histories, but how wonderful it is to think that God has forgiven us these things. How attractive Jesus is in this section! This woman—what a picture she presents! She was not cognizant of the stares around her, by which religious people are marked. Nobody stares at you, you know, so badly as a religious person, who thinks he is better than you are, or were. But there was no icy stare with Jesus. What a look Jesus would give this woman as she acted toward Him in an attitude which expressed her appreciation of the grace that reached and dealt with her sins, and gave her a link with the Saviour that entered into the expression of her love.

Because of what Simon did not do, and what, really, he could not do, she acted. She washed His feet with tears and wiped them with her hair. The Lord says to Simon, “Thou gavest me not a kiss, but she from the time I came in has not ceased kissing my feet. My head with oil thou didst not anoint, but she has anointed my feet with myrrh”. She never let up; she never ceased. It was not just a passing flash of attention that she paid to Jesus. She was deeply affected by the fact that the moral question, involving her sins, had been met by this Person, and she wanted to honour Him as He was worthy to be honoured, with all the affection she could lavish upon Him, Stranger of Galilee as He was to Simon the Pharisee. The Lord said, “For which cause I say to thee, Her many sins are forgiven; for she loved much; but he to whom little is forgiven loves little. And he said to her, Thy sins are forgiven”. What a message comes to us through Christ in the gospel this day, as we are convicted in regard to sins! What a touch it should be to any one of us! We should never lose the touch of our first knowledge of Christ and our contact with Him in relation to the matter of our sins, which the most of us would say were many.

Now I want to say a word as to the two malefactors. It is remarkable that we should have the two debtors to begin with in this gospel, and two malefactors at the end. What a scene it was at the cross! These malefactors were crucified with the Lord Jesus, one on one side and one on the other. But there is a difference that comes about; one is convicted, and the other is not. The one has reached a true judgment of himself. He says, in speaking to the other who spoke insultingly to Christ, “Dost thou too not fear God, thou that art under the same judgment? and we indeed justly, for we receive the just recompense of what we have done; but this man has done nothing amiss”. What an impression he had in his soul of the sinlessness of Jesus! How quickly he must have arrived at it, and how quickly the answer to his conviction was found. Quickly he gave expression to his conviction, and quickly an answer was found as he said to the Lord, “Remember me, Lord, when thou comest in thy kingdom”.

He must have gotten some impression of the kingdom of God and the Person of Jesus by his side. It is a wonderful thing to see that the kingdom of God involves forgiveness. That is the character it takes at the present time in the glad tidings, and this man gets an impression of the kingdom, and of the Lord as He was by his side, and he says, “Remember me, Lord, when thou comest in thy kingdom. And Jesus said to him, Verily I say to thee, Today shalt thou be with me in paradise”. How quickly the Lord answered the conviction that came about in this man! And that is what happens with any one of us. As we are convicted we will get a quick reply, as this man did. So he found his desire answered. Being a malefactor, he must have felt that it would be a great thing to be found in the kingdom of the Lord Jesus Christ. What a transfer it would be! It is a great thing to understand what we have been transferred from, and what we have been introduced into, as it says, we have been delivered “from the authority of darkness, and translated … into the kingdom of the Son of his love”, Colossians 1: 13. God is holding out, as it were, the best for us, in the kingdom of the Son of His love.

We need to be affected by the way Luke presents our deliverance from all that stood against us morally. And when we come to Luke’s further treatise (this is his first treatise; we have another in the book of the Acts), he brings in the coming of the Spirit. That is a great matter of the gospel, that not only have our sins been met and dealt with, and forgiveness conveyed to us, but God proposes—how wonderful He is!—that we should have not only the forgiveness of sins, but the gift of the Spirit. Thus we have the power to live as believers should live, in keeping with all that the presence of the Spirit of God means, no longer hindered or hampered by the sense of any sins being upon us, but happy and free, and full of joy in the sense that our sins have been forgiven, and that we have the gift of the Spirit, who gives us the assurance of our sins being forgiven.

Well, I desired just to refer to the wonderful way in which Luke presents the gospel, and the attractive touches that he gives in regard to persons such as these, and others throughout the gospel, who had peace through their links with Christ. We referred to the woman who touched the Lord’s garment. That is a wonderful thing, that she had the sense that power had gone out of her, and the Lord had the sense that power had gone out of Him. So there was a meeting point between these two things—power going out of the woman, and power going out of Christ and affecting her. Thus we have the assembly, not composed of persons who have just read verses or studied books, but persons who have been vitally affected by power being in them that came out of Christ. May God help us to see the value of the glad tidings in the light of these matters, as Luke presents them, for His name’s sake.

I want to speak, beloved brethren, about personal affection for the Lord Jesus and how He values it. I believe He values it more than anything with us. I have read these three scriptures because I believe they bring this out. You can see affection for Christ in its beginnings in the first scripture. In the second scripture we see affection for Christ in that great lover, Mary of Magdala, and lastly, in chapter 21, the great affection of John, the disciple whom Jesus loved. I believe that one of the main services of the Spirit today would be in relation to personal attachment to Christ, which the Lord values so much.

I want to engage your attention with this great matter, as bearing on us now, from this remarkable gospel. I think we can speak of it as the love gospel and is it not touching to think of it as written by the one who styles himself, “the disciple whom Jesus loved”. Right in the first chapter we have, “No one has seen God at any time; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him”, John 1: 18. The declaration of God has been by the One who is in the bosom of the Father; that is, in the place of love. When we come to chapter 3 we have, “The Father loves the Son, and has given all things to be in his hand”, John 3: 35. The Lord Jesus said Himself, “but that the world may know that I love the Father”, John 14: 31. Think of these statements as to love—how wonderful, how precious they are as we go on in the gospel.

In chapter 13 we get love’s precious service in the feet washing, a service that is to be continued amongst us, also the comment of the Spirit as to the Lord Jesus that He “having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end”. There is no question as to His love, beloved brethren, and every one in the close of this wonderful dispensation who is in the path of the will of God can be assured of the conscious sense of His love. A brother said amongst us a few weeks ago that we have intelligence; we have been so greatly helped through the ministry of the revival, bringing out in fulness the great thoughts of divine love; but it may be the lack with us is in love, that may be the challenge at the present time for all our hearts. I say it in regard to myself. O, may the Lord Jesus affect our hearts this afternoon more toward Himself!

Think of what is set out in these two disciples as they heard John the baptist speak. We think of John with affection—what a lover of Christ he was! Think of the holy admiration of John as he calls attention to Christ, speaking of Him first as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. Then he goes on to speak of Him as the One who baptises with the Holy Spirit, the Son of God. We come then to this third incident where it speaks of John “looking on Jesus as he walked”. O, the walk of Jesus, and what holy admiration there was in the heart of John! Was there ever a walk, beloved brethren, like the walk of Jesus? Think of the moral beauties and the perfection of the walk of Jesus.

Looking at Jesus as He walked he says, “Behold the Lamb of God”. This is the Object for our affections, beloved brethren, and here are five words with the understanding, as has often been said. John’s disciples were attracted and they followed. To me it is typified in the attractiveness of Noah in his position in the ark. The creatures, it says, “came two and two unto Noah into the ark”, Genesis 7: 9. Think of the wonderful attraction as these disciples of John followed Jesus! This gospel is full of the attractiveness of Christ, as He says Himself, “And I, if I be lifted up out of the earth, will draw all to me”, John 12: 32. Think of the drawing power of the attractiveness of Jesus as the two followed. He turned and saw them following and said, “What seek ye?” and they said, “Rabbi (which, being interpreted, signifies teacher), where abidest thou?”. They did not address Him as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, or as Son of God; they say, “Rabbi”. Their desire was to come under the teaching, and to come into His circumstances. The Lord Jesus says, “Come and see”. What an invitations and how He valued their affection. All true life would move to Him, that glorious Man. I think it would set out “Christ everything” (Colossians 3: 11), and the headship of Christ.

When we come to John 20, how full that chapter is, and how affecting it always is. Mary of Magdala, according to chapter 19, was one of the four who stood by the cross of Jesus, three sisters and one brother. I think the emphasis on the sisters, beloved brethren, would set out this great thought of affection for Christ. “The disciple standing by, whom he loved”, is very affecting to every lover of Christ. They stood by the cross of Christ. They were there in the most extreme circumstances. Beloved brethren, we have passed through many things, but love never fails (1 Corinthians 13: 8); love will stand in the most extreme circumstances. Mr. Taylor used that scripture in regard to localities where numbers are few, and what a word it is today, “love never fails”.

In chapter 20 we have Mary of Magdala, and on the first day of the week, very early in the morning while it was still dark, that great lover of Jesus comes to the tomb. She sees the stone is taken away and runs and tells Peter and John, lovers of Jesus. She came and told these disciples and they two ran together. John outruns Peter and, stooping down, he sees the linen cloths lying, but did not go in. It says that Peter came, following him, and went into the tomb and sees the linen cloths lying, and the handkerchief which was upon His head folded up in a distinct place by itself. John then entered in and he saw and believed, but then the disciples went away again to their own home. Think of the wonderful triumph of the death of Christ.

No disturbance, all is in order, but He out of death, the glorious Victor. That is how John presents it, the glory of the Person of Christ who has annulled death and brought to light life and incorruptibility by the glad tidings, (2 Timothy 1: 10).

Mary remained at the tomb weeping, and as she wept she stooped down into the tomb and beheld two angels sitting in white garments, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain. Two angels—O, the dignity of it! Think of the glory of the Person who had lain there, how worthy He is to be revered. They say to her, “Woman, why dost thou weep? She says to them, Because they have taken away my Lord, and I know not where they have laid him”. She, turning backward, sees Jesus and He says to her, “Woman, why dost thou weep?”. It was really, beloved, the morning of joy. Christ out of death. “Weeping cometh for the night, and at morn there is rejoicing”, Psalm 30: 5. It was the dawn, speaking simply, of the eternal morning. Mary, however, supposes Him to be the gardener. She says, “If thou hast borne him hence, tell me where thou hast laid him, and I will take him away”. Think of such affection for the Lord Jesus, “I will take him away”. We have often thought of that as a reference to loving with all her strength. Jesus says, “Mary”—the personal touch. She now turns round. She had been engaged with earthly things, supposing Him to be the gardener, but now she says, “Rabboni”—‘My Teacher’. Beloved brethren, how we need the teaching! The two at the beginning said, “Rabbi” or ‘Teacher’. What a remarkable gospel this is in its references to the teaching, and we need teaching to bring us into the greatest thoughts of divine love.

So Mary says, “Rabboni”, and the Lord Jesus says, “Touch me not, for I have not yet ascended to my Father; but go to my brethren and say to them, I ascend to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God”. How the Lord valued Mary, that great lover of Jesus, and to such love He gives the most precious things. He had committed His mother to John as he was standing by the cross, now He gives to Mary this wondrous message that so thrills our souls, bringing out the full truth of christianity. We used to speak much in earlier days of resurrection ground, but the full truth of christianity relates to ascension. “I ascend to my Father and your Father and to my God and your God”, involving association with Him in heavenly places in sonship. Mary, this great lover, gets the message.

How the Lord Jesus valued the personal affection of Mary! It says she came to the disciples and told them that “she had seen the Lord, and that he had said these things to her”. How comely is her behaviour! There was no parading of what Jesus had said to her; nothing to draw attention to herself in that sense. It reminds me of the scripture as to love, that it “does not behave in an unseemly manner”, 1 Corinthians 13: 5. Here is love behaving in a comely, beautiful way.

Now I want to go on to what is said of John in this last chapter, which is, as we have been taught, a kind of appendix to the gospel. The chapter is bringing out the service of the Lord Jesus in relation to His own in recovery. Are we not interested in that?—for we are all recovered persons here, recovered to the truth in its preciousness and fulness. Thank God it is through the personal service of the Lord Jesus. How touching that is! Here we have the third manifestation of Jesus in resurrection, and it is in relation to seven erring brothers. Peter says, “I go to fish”; the others say, “We also come with thee”. That is a party. The Lord Jesus operates in wondrous grace to meet that. O, how we need to see the skill, the amazing skill, of the Lord Jesus, the grace of the position, as it says in chapter 1, “of his fulness we all have received, and grace upon grace”. It has been said that that is this chapter, grace upon grace, and have we not known, dear brethren, the Lord Jesus in His wondrous service in recovery?

Then we go on to the adjusting of Peter, the adjusting of the servant, the probing of Peter, to the and that the lambs shall be fed, the sheep shepherded, and the sheep fed. These were the matters the Lord Jesus committed to Peter as he probed him as to his personal affection for Him. The Lord Jesus told Peter what would come when he was old. He would be brought where he did not desire. This He said “signifying by what death he should glorify God”. Think of what Peter was brought to in submission to the will of God, so that.in his death he would glorify God.

It goes on, however, to show us here that Peter was momentarily deflected. Jesus said to him, “Follow me”. Peter, turning round, sees John following. We need to guard against this, beloved brethren. We need to guard against concern about one another in this way. “What of this man?”. A person who is following is safe; we can, in the sense in which this is presented, leave him to the Lord Jesus. Let us go on filling out the part and the place that He has given us; that is the truth at the close of this wonderful gospel of John. It speaks of John leaning on the breast of Jesus. Think of what is available to us, this near place, near to Christ as in His affections. Leaning on His breast John availed himself of what was available there. We can all have that near place, near to Christ. John was preserved; he goes forward, filling out the part that the Lord had given him. Jesus said to Peter rebukingly, “If I will that he abide until I come, what is that to thee? Follow thou me”. That is a word to us this afternoon, beloved brethren. Let us not be concerned about one another in this sense. Let no rivalry come in. The Lord Jesus is operating against it. What a baneful thing it has been in the history of the revival; let it not come into our localities.

As John is following, he is in his place. John is the reserve man. In his ministry he ‘abides’. John writes for the last days and his ministry is bearing on us now. He is conscious of the place he has; he says, “This is the disciple … who has written these things; and we know that his witness is true”. He was a true follower and a true lover of Jesus, and how the Lord Jesus valued it. The reserve man, that is John’s place, and he goes on to speak of wonderful reserves, that the things which Jesus did, if they were written one by one, “I suppose that not even the world itself would contain the books written”. Sufficient has been written; all that is needed has been written. As John says earlier, “These are written that ye may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing ye might have life in his name”, John 20: 31. That is the end for which this gospel is written, that we may believe in the divine Operator, in the Son of God, who has brought in a system which abides eternally. That is what every lover of Christ should have before him.

I say again, we are nearing the end of this wonderful dispensation; the Spirit’s lowly, patient service is almost completed. We have been speaking earlier of walking with God and of the fact that “the Spirit and the bride say, Come”, Revelation 22: 17. That is the completion of this wonderful dispensation. The bride represents fully developed affections for Christ. Mary of Magdala is a figure of what Christ loves, we may say, above all. His supreme joy as Man is the assembly. How precious these things are, beloved brethren! May we love the Lord Jesus increasingly. How worthy He is of it! You dear young people, think of the attractiveness of the Lord Jesus! O, may you follow, and may you feel in your hearts that wonderful invitation, “Come and see”! May it be so, for His name’s sake.

I have in mind to say a few words on the thought of being faithful. The last verse of the first scripture I read is one that imparts tremendous stability, that in the presence of so much unfaithfulness there is a glorious Person who abides faithful. Indeed the very darkness of the background but brings out the lustre of the glory of the Person of whom it is said, “He abides faithful, for he cannot deny himself”. What a rock on which to rest, the fact that, no matter what comes in, He abides faithful. May God strengthen all our hearts in this.

When John was in Patmos he looked at the stability of God’s throne, and at the power that there is to maintain its rights, but then he refers to the answer there has been here below in the faithful Witness (Revelation 1: 5). How wonderful to know that, in a scene of so much unfaithfulness, there has been a faithful Witness for God. It is in the light of this that he goes on to refer to Him in His own glorious greatness. Would that our hearts might increasingly join in that doxology, “To him who loves us”. The unchangeable love of Jesus remains in spite of everything, and is the surety and certainty that all for our joy and for God’s pleasure will be secured, “If we are unfaithful, he abides faithful”.

There are other references to faithfulness in this chapter in Timothy. The testimony is to be entrusted to “faithful men, such as shall be competent to instruct others also”. I would encourage us that that is what is needed at the present time, the element of faithfulness in relation to the truth. Through Paul God would remind this young man Timothy of the stability and power that are in His things, “Be strong in the grace which is in Christ Jesus”. It is a wonderful thing to get our hearts lifted up to think of all that is resident in that glorious Man where He is, a nail in a sure place, and to know that there is abounding grace for the present position of the testimony, flowing from Him there. Paul says in another place, “My God shall abundantly supply all your need according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4: 19)—wonderful source of supply and power for the testimony at all times. May our hearts be strengthened to realise this power, which is adequate to carry us through right to the end.

Then the passage comes on to the reason why the Lord has taken us up. It is to be good soldiers. Christianity is not a voluntary matter. It is a question of having been enlisted, and of recognising who has enlisted you. He takes on what may appear to be pretty poor material, but we would be encouraged and strengthened to be ‘good soldiers of Jesus Christ’, persons who are not entangled with the affairs of life. Beloved, may I speak very simply. What engages and occupies my mind? What is the primary consideration of my life? Am I here to please the One who has enlisted me? I think some of us who were ‘called up’ in the war may have had in experience advantage over some younger persons. In those conditions you could not get too entangled with the affairs of life. You just had to do what the commanding officer wanted. God would have us to know what it is to be enlisted by this glorious Person and that we might increasingly realise that He has enlisted us, in view of being here in His testimony.

Then we are to contend in the games lawfully. I believe there are some who try to take short cuts. The result is that they never finish the course. There is a way into spiritual things, and God would have us to go that way. Man’s natural ability is of no avail in divine things. We have to see that God has set aside, everything that stands related to me as born of Adam’s race. Instead He would establish me in another Man, and give me another power altogether, in the consciousness of the Holy Spirit indwelling. We are to contend in the games lawfully, and to be persons who are finishing the course. As Paul says later on, there is a crown of righteousness laid up for all that love His appearing. May we be persons who have the finishing of the course before us, as numbered amongst those who are loving His appearing.

Paul speaks of the husbandman labouring in view of fruit. No matter where we are at the present time, it is not a time for settling down, beloved. It is a time of labour, a time of energy, in view of fruit. May God encourage our hearts that we may be in the testimony in a vital way as committing ourselves unreservedly in the light of the glorious Person who, even if everyone else were unfaithful, remains faithful.
Even to Laodicea He says, “I rebuke and discipline as many as I love”, Revelation 3; 19. It is the faithfulness of His love, love that can be relied upon, strength that can be relied upon.

The scripture in Luke is a very sobering one, the Lord warning His own as to the leaven of hypocrisy. We live in a day when so much appears to be other than what it really is, when things are different underneath from what they appear to be on the surface. The chapter ends with the Lord referring to certain persons as hypocrites, as not discerning the time. God would have us to discern what the time is. We are right at the close of the dispensation. The coming of the Lord is an immediate matter. Some of us were reminded on Lord’s day that in just a moment we shall be taken out of the scene of time, of worry, of trial, and of suffering, and we shall be ever with the Lord. We are on the verge of these things, beloved. There is a peculiar urgency, a need to be watching, as the Lord mentions in this scripture. Earlier in the chapter He shows how persons tend to be engaged with the things of this world. He speaks in the parable about a person whom God refers to as a fool, one who is spending his time amassing things in this scene and, as He says, is not rich towards God. It is a time when we should all be becoming enriched towards God. Whatever we amass of things here below we shall leave behind. Mr. Raven said that the most humbling thing is not that things leave us but that we leave them.
At the same time the Lord goes on to speak about the very hairs of our head being numbered.

O, beloved, that we might be more in the consciousness of what we are to God! God numbers the very hairs of our head. How little interest sometimes we may have in God, but God is wonderfully interested in us at all times. The Lord speaks about the sparrows, and says, “Ye are better than many sparrows” (Luke 12: 7). He speaks about the grass. He speaks about the ravens, He speaks about the way God cares for us. Why should we be in anxiety? There is plenty of anxiety around as to what is going to happen. The days we are in have the very character of the days spoken of in this chapter, but God would have us to be restful, and have our treasure not down here, but in the heavens. That is what is in mind in the reference to the birds, that God would have us to understand that we are heavenly persons.

Then there is this word, “Who then is the faithful and prudent steward?”. The Lord would direct the word to hearer and speaker alike. He would challenge all of us as to what we are using the present time for, whether we are using it in His service. What wonderful promises there are in this chapter to those who are found watching. He says, “He … will make them recline at table, and coming up will serve them”. How gloriously attractive it is to be served by Christ! We have all been served by Him, but He promises, so to speak, to give His own special service to persons who are found watching. The question is raised, “Who is the faithful and prudent steward?”. The Lord would encourage us to qualify for that, that we might be persons who are restful in their spirits, not needing to worry about what we are going to put on (How much time we may spend doing that!), or what we are going to eat.

Instead, He would have us devote the little time we have left to the service of His people, to being persons who are providing spiritual food in its season, who know what the Master’s mind is, and bring it in. What an opportunity is afforded each Tuesday to most of us brothers, just to bring in food in its season, being with the Lord in relation to the current need in our own localities and bringing food in. He says, “He will set him over all that he has”. I believe this is the training time in view of the day of administration. May we be faithful and prudent stewards who are concerned to provide for the Lord’s household just what is needed.

In the scripture in Acts we have a man under direction, a sensitive man. He is prevented by the Spirit from going in one direction, but then the Spirit of Jesus comes in to direct him in another. At the close of this dispensation the Lord is concerned about finding a sensitive area of things, such as Philippi speaks of. It stands in contrast to all we find in the world around. It is a sphere where what is excellent is not good enough. He says, “That ye may judge of and approve the things that are more excellent”, Philippians 1: 10. It is a sphere of things where there are “bowels and compassions”, Philippians 2: 1. It is marked by peace, the peace of God, and the God of peace. It is a sphere of abundant supplies, as has already been said, but it is also an area of things where persons are working out their own salvation in fear and trembling. The Lord is looking for an answer here below to the truth, where things are according to His own mind. It is to be found amongst persons whose hearts have been opened to receive the things spoken by Paul, and who are attending to them. Just to hear the things spoken by Paul is not sufficient, we must attend to them.

Because of what we are, there is ever a tendency with us to become casual in our attitude to details connected with God’s things, whereas Paul speaks in the Philippian epistle of his feelings in relation to persons glorying in their shame and who mind earthly things. In his approach to the Lord’s supper in Corinthians he touches on various practical matters relating to the deportment of men and women, such as the token, the covering, and length of hair to be worn by each. It is right for us to feel it where such directions are ignored. Faithfulness to the Lord is involved in our attending to these matters and refusing to be governed as to them by the changing fashion of a passing world where He was crucified. We need to be regulated by the things spoken by Paul if we are to know what truly belongs to christianity.

Lydia says, “If ye have judged me to be faithful to the Lord”. Let us come under scrutiny and searching as to whether we have been faithful to the Lord in relation to the ministry that Paul has set on. Are things right with me? Are they right in my household? Are they right in the locality? I am not suggesting harshness. In dealing with these things, the answer is the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ. But let us be concerned to be marked as persons who are faithful to the Lord in relation to the ministry of Paul. God would help us in it, for He wants to bring us fully into this wonderful area of things where christianity is known and experienced.

Just read the epistle to the Philippians again. What an attractive area! The glorious resource of it is that faithful One, and the mind that was in Him is to be in us, by way of regulation, the mind to go down. It is a wonderfully attractive scene into which God would introduce us, but it is reached by persons who are faithful to the Lord. May God help us to see that the stability of everything is the faithfulness of the Lord Jesus. In answer to it, may we spend the rest of our time in faithfulness to Him. May we know what it is to serve the saints in faithfulness, and may we all be among those who “attend to the things spoken by Paul”, for the pleasure of God and for His glory.

There is nothing we meet with more commonly than two Christians forming diverse judgments about the same thing. Is it man’s mind looking at the thing, or God’s? Instead of being very ready to give an opinion, first see whether you are with the Lord about it. Be in a right state, and then you will see His mind. When God wants to tell you anything, He must put you where there is nothing to interfere with His communications; He cannot communicate where there is interference with His dealings.
